title: I Thought My Slides Helped Students Learn. Turns Out, They’re Doing More Harm Than Good.
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: A teacher reflects on how reading Oliver Lovell's Cognitive Load Theory in Action changed his view of his own slide decks. He explains the modality effect, that spreading load across visual and auditory channels frees working memory, and shows how his text-heavy slides read aloud were overloading students. He then covers two traps, the transient information effect and the redundancy effect, noting that reading on-screen text aloud makes learning harder. His changes include using more visuals, pointing while talking, letting students read before he explains, and giving written summaries. The article is a candid, applied translation of cognitive load theory into presentation practice.
points: The modality effect holds that explaining aloud over a related visual spreads load across two channels, unlike reading text aloud.
Reading slide text aloud triggers the redundancy effect and competes for the same channel.
Verbal and visual information should be unintelligible in isolation so each depends on the other.
Transient spoken or visual information needs a written summary or reference visual so students need not hold it in memory.
Concrete changes include pointing, look here listen now prompts, and pausing so students can read first.
quotes: One idea that really stuck with me is the modality effect. It’s not complicated. It just means students learn better when you explain something out loud while showing a related visual, instead of dumping everything into text or talking over a block of writing.

But if I show a diagram or picture and talk through it, now we’re spreading the same cognitive load across both the visual and auditory channels. That’s basically what the modality effect is: saying it + showing it.

If I’m talking about the boundaries of a city changing because of urban sprawl, I’ll literally point to it on the map. It helps focus their attention and reduces confusion between what they are seeing and hearing.
If there’s substantial text on the screen, I’ll pause and let students read it first, then I’ll talk about it, using different words to explain the big ideas.
When I read the same text that’s already on the slide, I’m not reinforcing the info, I’m making it harder to learn. That’s the redundancy effect.

If I explain something out loud or show a visual that’s important for students to refer to later, I’ll also give them a short written version or copy of the visual with a summary in their booklet. That way, they don’t have to hold everything in working memory.
